# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [AnyBit](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)- Pattern
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types that are valid for any bit pattern.
- [Contiguous](https://docs.rs/trait.Contiguous.html)
- A trait indicating that:
- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data” types with no uninit (or padding) bytes.
- [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)
- Marker trait for “plain old data”.
- [PodIn](https://docs.rs/trait.PodInOption.html)- Option
- Trait for types which are [Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).
- [Transparent](https://docs.rs/trait.TransparentWrapper.html)- Wrapper
- A trait which indicates that a type is a `#[repr(transparent)]`wrapper around the`Inner`value.
- [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)
- Trait for types that can be safely created with
`zeroed`

- Trait for types which are [Zeroable](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)when wrapped in[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of.html)- of
- Re-interprets `&T`as`&[u8]`.
- [bytes_](https://docs.rs/fn.bytes_of_mut.html)- of_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut T`as`&mut [u8]`.
- [cast](https://docs.rs/fn.cast.html)
- Cast `A`into`B`
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_mut.html)- mut
- Cast `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_ref.html)- ref
- Cast `&A`into`&B`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice.html)- slice
- Cast `&[A]`into`&[B]`.
- [cast_](https://docs.rs/fn.cast_slice_mut.html)- slice_ - mut
- Cast `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`.
- [fill_](https://docs.rs/fn.fill_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `slice`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes.html)- bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [from_](https://docs.rs/fn.from_bytes_mut.html)- bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast.html)- cast - `must_cast`
- Cast `A`into`B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref - `must_cast`
- Convert `&A`into`&B`if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice - `must_cast`
- Convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [must_](https://docs.rs/fn.must_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut - `must_cast`
- Convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length) if infalliable, or fail to compile.
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to.html)- align_ - to
- As `align_to``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_align_to_mut.html)- align_ - to_ - mut
- As `align_to_mut``Pod`
- [pod_](https://docs.rs/fn.pod_read_unaligned.html)- read_ - unaligned
- Reads the slice into a `T`value.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast.html)- cast
- Try to cast `A`into`B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_mut.html)- cast_ - mut
- Try to convert a `&mut A`into`&mut B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_ref.html)- cast_ - ref
- Try to convert a `&A`into`&B`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice.html)- cast_ - slice
- Try to convert `&[A]`into`&[B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_cast_slice_mut.html)- cast_ - slice_ - mut
- Try to convert `&mut [A]`into`&mut [B]`(possibly with a change in length).
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes.html)- from_ - bytes
- Re-interprets `&[u8]`as`&T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_from_bytes_mut.html)- from_ - bytes_ - mut
- Re-interprets `&mut [u8]`as`&mut T`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/fn.try_pod_read_unaligned.html)- pod_ - read_ - unaligned
- Reads from the bytes as if they were a `T`.
- [write_](https://docs.rs/fn.write_zeroes.html)- zeroes
- Fill all bytes of `target`with zeroes (see`Zeroable`
- [zeroed](https://docs.rs/fn.zeroed.html)- `const_zeroed`
- Same as `Zeroable::zeroed``const fn`const.

# EncodedSrgb in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.EncodedSrgb.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct EncodedSrgb<ComponentTy = `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the encoded sRGB color space.

This color space uses the sRGB/Rec.709 primaries, D65 white point, and sRGB transfer functions. The encoded version is nonlinear, with the sRGB OETF, aka “gamma compensation”, applied.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

`r: ComponentTy`The red component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.g)

`g: ComponentTy`The green component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.b)

`b: ComponentTy`The blue component.

# LinearSrgb in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.LinearSrgb.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct LinearSrgb<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the linear (decoded) sRGB color space.

This color space uses the sRGB/Rec.709 primaries, D65 white point,
and sRGB transfer functions. This version is linear, with the
sRGB EOTF, aka “inverse gamma compensation”, applied in order to
decode it from `EncodedSrgb`

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.r)

`r: ComponentTy`The red component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.g)

`g: ComponentTy`The green component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.b)

`b: ComponentTy`The blue component.

    pub x: ComponentTy,
    pub y: ComponentTy,
    pub z: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in a generic color space that can be represented by 3 components. The user is responsible for ensuring that the correct color space is respected.

# Spaces in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/enum.Spaces.html

```
#[repr(u32)]pub enum Spaces {
```
## Show 36 variants

    EncodedSrgb = 0,
    LinearSrgb = 1,
    EncodedRec709 = 2,
    Rec709 = 3,
    GenericColor3 = 4,
    GenericColor1 = 5,
    Luminance = 6,
    Luma = 7,
    AcesCg = 8,
    Aces2065 = 9,
    AcesCc = 10,
    AcesCct = 11,
    DisplayP3 = 12,
    EncodedDisplayP3 = 13,
    DciP3 = 14,
    DciXYZPrime = 15,
    Bt2020 = 16,
    EncodedBt2020 = 17,
    Bt2100 = 18,
    EncodedBt2100PQ = 19,
    EncodedBt2100HLG = 20,
    ICtCpPQ = 21,
    ICtCpHLG = 22,
    CieXYZ = 23,
    CieLab = 24,
    CieLCh = 25,
    Oklab = 26,
    Oklch = 27,
    Hsl = 28,
    Hsv = 29,
    YCbCr = 30,
    YPrimeCbCr = 31,
    YPbPr = 32,
    YPrimePbPr = 33,
    Yuv = 34,
    YCxCz = 35,
}## Expand description

An enum with a variant for each of the color spaces supported by the library. Useful for tracking as metadata in something like an image type, and for runtime-determined color types.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedSrgb)

### EncodedSrgb = 0

A color in the encoded sRGB color space.

This color space uses the sRGB/Rec.709 primaries, D65 white point, and sRGB transfer functions. The encoded version is nonlinear, with the sRGB OETF, aka “gamma compensation”, applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.LinearSrgb)

### LinearSrgb = 1

A color in the linear (decoded) sRGB color space.

This color space uses the sRGB/Rec.709 primaries, D65 white point,
and sRGB transfer functions. This version is linear, with the
sRGB EOTF, aka “inverse gamma compensation”, applied in order to
decode it from `EncodedSrgb`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedRec709)

### EncodedRec709 = 2

A color in the encoded Rec.709/BT.709 color space.

This color space uses the BT.709 primaries, D65 white point, and BT.601 (reused in BT.709) transfer function. The encoded version is nonlinear, with the BT.601 OETF applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Rec709)

### Rec709 = 3

A color in the Rec.709/BT.709 color space.

This color space uses the BT.709 primaries, D65 white point, and BT.601 (reused in BT.709) transfer function. This version is linear, without the BT.601 OETF applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.GenericColor3)

### GenericColor3 = 4

A color in a generic color space that can be represented by 3 components. The user is responsible for ensuring that the correct color space is respected.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.GenericColor1)

### GenericColor1 = 5

A color in a generic color space that can be represented by 1 component. The user is responsible for ensuring that the correct color space is respected.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Luminance)

### Luminance = 6

A single-channel CIE luminance.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Luma)

### Luma = 7

A single-channel CIE luma (non-linear transform from luminance).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AcesCg)

### AcesCg = 8

A color in the ACEScg color space.

This color space uses the ACES AP1 primaries and D60 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Aces2065)

### Aces2065 = 9

A color in the ACES 2065-1 color space.

This color space uses the ACES AP0 primaries and D60 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AcesCc)

### AcesCc = 10

A color in the ACEScc color space.

This color space uses the ACES AP1 primaries and D60 white point and a pure logarithmic transfer function.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AcesCct)

### AcesCct = 11

A color in the ACEScct color space.

This color space uses the ACES AP1 primaries and D60 white point and a logarithmic transfer function with a toe such that values are able to go negative.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DisplayP3)

### DisplayP3 = 12

A color in the Display P3 (aka P3 D65) color space.

This color space uses the P3 primaries and D65 white point and sRGB transfer functions. This version is linear, without the sRGB OETF applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedDisplayP3)

### EncodedDisplayP3 = 13

A color in the Display P3 (aka P3 D65) color space.

This color space uses the P3 primaries and D65 white point and sRGB transfer functions. This encoded version is nonlinear, with the sRGB OETF applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DciP3)

### DciP3 = 14

A color in the DCI-P3 (aka P3 DCI and P3 D60) color space.

If you are looking for the P3 which is used on new Apple displays, see
[ DisplayP3](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayP3.html) instead.

This color space uses the P3 primaries and D60 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.DciXYZPrime)

### DciXYZPrime = 15

A color in the X’Y’Z’ color space, a DCI specification used for digital cinema mastering.

This color space uses the CIE XYZ primaries, with special DCI white point and pure 2.6 gamma encoding.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Bt2020)

### Bt2020 = 16

A color in the BT.2020 color space.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedBt2020)

### EncodedBt2020 = 17

A color in the encoded BT.2020 color space.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point and the BT.2020 transfer functions (equivalent to BT.601 transfer functions but with higher precision). This encoded version is nonlinear, with the BT.2020/BT.601 OETF applied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Bt2100)

### Bt2100 = 18

A color in the BT.2100 color space.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedBt2100PQ)

### EncodedBt2100PQ = 19

A color in the encoded BT.2100 color space with PQ (Perceptual Quantizer) transfer function.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point and the ST 2084/“PQ” transfer function. It is nonlinear.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.EncodedBt2100HLG)

### EncodedBt2100HLG = 20

A color in the encoded BT.2100 color space with HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) transfer function.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point and the HLG transfer function. It is nonlinear.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ICtCpPQ)

### ICtCpPQ = 21

A color in the ICtCp color space with PQ (Perceptual Quantizer) nonlinearity.

This color space is based on the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point, but is not an RGB color space. Instead it is a roughly perceptual color space meant to more efficiently encode HDR content.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ICtCpHLG)

### ICtCpHLG = 22

A color in the ICtCp color space with HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) nonlinearity.

This color space is based on the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point, but is not an RGB color space. Instead it is a roughly perceptual color space meant to more efficiently encode HDR content.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CieXYZ)

### CieXYZ = 23

A color in the CIE XYZ color space.

This color space uses the CIE XYZ primaries and D65 white point.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CieLab)

### CieLab = 24

A color in the CIE L*a*b* color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.CieLCh)

### CieLCh = 25

A color in the CIE L*C*h° color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Oklab)

### Oklab = 26

A color in the Oklab color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Oklch)

### Oklch = 27

A color in the Oklch color space (a transformation from Oklab to LCh° coordinates).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Hsl)

### Hsl = 28

A color in the HSL color space.

Since HSL is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as the linear sRGB space, as that is the most common case.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Hsv)

### Hsv = 29

A color in the HSV color space.

Since HSV is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as the linear sRGB space, as that is the most common case.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YCbCr)

### YCbCr = 30

A color in the YCbCr color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr, YUV, and
YPbPr in [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

Since YCbCr is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as being converted from the LinearSrgb color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YPrimeCbCr)

### YPrimeCbCr = 31

A color in the Y’CbCr color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr, Y’CbCr,
YUV, YPbPr, and Y’PbPr in the [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

Since Y’CbCr is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as being converted from the EncodedSrgb color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YPbPr)

### YPbPr = 32

A color in the YPbPr color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr,
YUV, YPbPr, and Y’PbPr in the [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

Since YPbPr is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as being converted from the LinearSrgb color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YPrimePbPr)

### YPrimePbPr = 33

A color in the Y’PbPr color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr,
YUV, YPbPr, and Y’PbPr in the [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

Since Y’PbPr is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as being converted from the EncodedSrgb color space.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Yuv)

### Yuv = 34

A color in the YUV color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr, YUV, and
YPbPr in [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.YCxCz)

### YCxCz = 35

A color in the YCxCz (also called YyCxCz) color space, originally defined in “Optimized universal color palette design for error diffusion” by B. W. Kolpatzik and C. A. Bouman. Can be thought of as a “linear CIE Lab”.

# ColorInterop in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/trait.ColorInterop.html

```
pub trait ColorInterop{
    type
```
[CintTy](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.CintTy): [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<Self>;
    // Provided methods
    fn [from_cint](https://docs.rs#method.from_cint)(col: Self::[CintTy](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorInterop.html#associatedtype.CintTy)) -> Self { ... }
[into_cint](https://docs.rs#method.into_cint)(self) -> Self::[CintTy](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorInterop.html#associatedtype.CintTy) { ... }
}## Expand description

A trait that should be implemented by provider crates on their local color types so that you can call
`color.to_cint()` and `Color::from_cint(cint_color)`.

Provider crates should also do relevant `From`/`Into` impls, but [ ColorInterop](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorInterop.html) provides a “canonical”
transformation to the closest

`cint` color type.## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# PremultipliedAlpha in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.PremultipliedAlpha.html

`pub struct PremultipliedAlpha<ColorTy: `[ColorType](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorType.html)> {
    pub color: ColorTy,
    pub alpha: ColorTy::[ComponentTy](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorType.html#associatedtype.ComponentTy),
}## Expand description

A premultiplied color with an alpha component.

The color components have been premultiplied by the alpha component.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.color)

`color: ColorTy`The contained color, which has been premultiplied with `alpha`

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.alpha)

`alpha: ColorTy::`[ComponentTy](https://docs.rs/trait.ColorType.html#associatedtype.ComponentTy)The alpha component.

    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the ACEScct color space.

This color space uses the ACES AP1 primaries and D60 white point and a logarithmic transfer function with a toe such that values are able to go negative.

# DciXYZPrime in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.DciXYZPrime.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct DciXYZPrime<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub x: ComponentTy,
    pub y: ComponentTy,
    pub z: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the X’Y’Z’ color space, a DCI specification used for digital cinema mastering.

This color space uses the CIE XYZ primaries, with special DCI white point and pure 2.6 gamma encoding.

# EncodedBt2020 in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.EncodedBt2020.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct EncodedBt2020<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the encoded BT.2020 color space.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point and the BT.2020 transfer functions (equivalent to BT.601 transfer functions but with higher precision). This encoded version is nonlinear, with the BT.2020/BT.601 OETF applied.

# EncodedBt2100HLG in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.EncodedBt2100HLG.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct EncodedBt2100HLG<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the encoded BT.2100 color space with HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) transfer function.

This color space uses the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point and the HLG transfer function. It is nonlinear.

# EncodedDisplayP3 in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.EncodedDisplayP3.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct EncodedDisplayP3<ComponentTy = `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the Display P3 (aka P3 D65) color space.

This color space uses the P3 primaries and D65 white point and sRGB transfer functions. This encoded version is nonlinear, with the sRGB OETF applied.

# EncodedRec709 in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.EncodedRec709.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct EncodedRec709<ComponentTy = `[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the encoded Rec.709/BT.709 color space.

This color space uses the BT.709 primaries, D65 white point, and BT.601 (reused in BT.709) transfer function. The encoded version is nonlinear, with the BT.601 OETF applied.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.r)

`r: ComponentTy`The red component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.g)

`g: ComponentTy`The green component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.b)

`b: ComponentTy`The blue component.

# Hsv in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.Hsv.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct Hsv<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub h: ComponentTy,
    pub s: ComponentTy,
    pub v: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the HSV color space.

Since HSV is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as the linear sRGB space, as that is the most common case.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.h)

`h: ComponentTy`The H (hue) component. Varies from 0 to 1.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.s)

`s: ComponentTy`The S (saturation) component. Varies from 0 to 1.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.v)

`v: ComponentTy`The V (value) component. Varies from 0 to 1.

# ICtCpHLG in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.ICtCpHLG.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct ICtCpHLG<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub i: ComponentTy,
    pub ct: ComponentTy,
    pub cp: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the ICtCp color space with HLG (Hybrid Log-Gamma) nonlinearity.

This color space is based on the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point, but is not an RGB color space. Instead it is a roughly perceptual color space meant to more efficiently encode HDR content.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.i)

`i: ComponentTy`The I (intensity) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.ct)

`ct: ComponentTy`The Ct (chroma-tritan) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.cp)

`cp: ComponentTy`The Cp (chroma-protan) component.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cint/lib.rs.html#294-743)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-PartialOrd-for-ICtCpHLG%3CComponentTy%3E)### impl<ComponentTy: [PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)> [PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) for [ICtCpHLG](https://docs.rs/struct.ICtCpHLG.html)<ComponentTy>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/cint/lib.rs.html#294-743)

# ICtCpPQ in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.ICtCpPQ.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct ICtCpPQ<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub i: ComponentTy,
    pub ct: ComponentTy,
    pub cp: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the ICtCp color space with PQ (Perceptual Quantizer) nonlinearity.

This color space is based on the BT.2020 primaries and D65 white point, but is not an RGB color space. Instead it is a roughly perceptual color space meant to more efficiently encode HDR content.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.i)

`i: ComponentTy`The I (intensity) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.ct)

`ct: ComponentTy`The Ct (chroma-tritan) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.cp)

`cp: ComponentTy`The Cp (chroma-protan) component.

A color in the Oklch color space (a transformation from Oklab to LCh° coordinates).

# Rec709 in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.Rec709.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct Rec709<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub r: ComponentTy,
    pub g: ComponentTy,
    pub b: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the Rec.709/BT.709 color space.

This color space uses the BT.709 primaries, D65 white point, and BT.601 (reused in BT.709) transfer function. This version is linear, without the BT.601 OETF applied.

# YCxCz in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.YCxCz.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct YCxCz<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub y: ComponentTy,
    pub cx: ComponentTy,
    pub cz: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the YCxCz (also called YyCxCz) color space, originally defined in “Optimized universal color palette design for error diffusion” by B. W. Kolpatzik and C. A. Bouman. Can be thought of as a “linear CIE Lab”.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.y)

`y: ComponentTy`The Yy (luminance) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.cx)

`cx: ComponentTy`The Cx (chroma difference blue/yellow) component

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.cz)

`cz: ComponentTy`The Cz (chroma difference red/green) component

# YPrimePbPr in cint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/cint/^0.3.1/struct.YPrimePbPr.html

`#[repr(C)]pub struct YPrimePbPr<ComponentTy = `[f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.f32.html)> {
    pub y: ComponentTy,
    pub pb: ComponentTy,
    pub pr: ComponentTy,
}## Expand description

A color in the Y’PbPr color space. See discussion of the difference between YCbCr,
YUV, YPbPr, and Y’PbPr in the [YCbCr Wikipedia article](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YCbCr)

Since Y’PbPr is a relative color space, it is required to know the RGB space which it was transformed from. We define this as being converted from the EncodedSrgb color space.

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.y)

`y: ComponentTy`The Y’ (luma) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.pb)

`pb: ComponentTy`The Pb (chroma-blue/yellow) component.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.pr)

`pr: ComponentTy`The Pr (chroma-red/green) component.

# num-traits 0.2.19 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/num-traits/0.2.19

# num-traits

Numeric traits for generic mathematics in Rust.

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
```
## Features

This crate can be used without the standard library (`#![no_std]`) by disabling
the default `std` feature. Use this in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.2"
 = false
# features = ["libm"]    # <--- Uncomment if you wish to use `Float` and `Real` without `std`
```
The `Float` and `Real` traits are only available when either `std` or `libm` is enabled.

The `FloatCore` trait is always available.  `MulAdd` and `MulAddAssign` for `f32`
and `f64` also require `std` or `libm`, as do implementations of signed and floating-
point exponents in `Pow`.

## Releases

Release notes are available in [RELEASES.md](https://docs.rs/RELEASES.md).

## Compatibility

The `num-traits` crate is tested for rustc 1.60 and greater.

## License

Licensed under either of

at your option.

### Contribution

Unless you explicitly state otherwise, any contribution intentionally submitted for inclusion in the work by you, as defined in the Apache-2.0 license, shall be dual licensed as above, without any additional terms or conditions.

---

# autocfg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/autocfg/^1/

## Expand description

A Rust library for build scripts to automatically configure code based on
compiler support.  Code snippets are dynamically tested to see if the `rustc`
will accept them, rather than hard-coding specific version support.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[build-dependencies]
autocfg = "1"
```
Then use it in your `build.rs` script to detect compiler features.  For
example, to test for 128-bit integer support, it might look like:

```
extern crate autocfg;
fn main() {
    let ac = autocfg::new();
    ac.emit_has_type("i128");
    // (optional) We don't need to rerun for anything external.
    autocfg::rerun_path("build.rs");
}
```
If the type test succeeds, this will write a `cargo:rustc-cfg=has_i128` line
for Cargo, which translates to Rust arguments `--cfg has_i128`.  Then in the
rest of your Rust code, you can add `#[cfg(has_i128)]` conditions on code that
should only be used when the compiler supports it.

[§](https://docs.rs#caution)Caution

Many of the probing methods of `AutoCfg` document the particular template they
use, **subject to change**. The inputs are not validated to make sure they are
semantically correct for their expected use, so it’s *possible* to escape and
inject something unintended. However, such abuse is unsupported and will not
be considered when making changes to the templates.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AutoCfg](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoCfg.html)
- Helper to detect compiler features for `cfg`output in build scripts.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)
- A common error type for the `autocfg`crate.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [emit](https://docs.rs/fn.emit.html)
- Writes a config flag for rustc on standard out.
- [emit_](https://docs.rs/fn.emit_possibility.html)- possibility
- Indicates to rustc that a config flag should not generate an `unexpected_cfgs`warning
- [new](https://docs.rs/fn.new.html)
- Creates a new `AutoCfg`instance.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_env.html)- env
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if the environment
variable `var`changes.
- [rerun_](https://docs.rs/fn.rerun_path.html)- path
- Writes a line telling Cargo to rerun the build script if `path`changes.

# Num in num_traits - Rust

pub trait Num:

    + [Zero](https://docs.rs/identities/trait.Zero.html)

}## Expand description

The base trait for numeric types, covering `0` and `1` values,
comparisons, basic numeric operations, and string conversion.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_traits/lib.rs.html#95)#### fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_str_radix)(str: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/num_traits/lib.rs.html#95)

#### fn [from_str_radix](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_str_radix)(str: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html), radix: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<Self, Self::[FromStrRadixErr](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html#associatedtype.FromStrRadixErr)>

Convert from a string and radix (typically `2..=36`).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use num_traits::Num;
let result = <i32 as Num>::from_str_radix("27", 10);
assert_eq!(result, Ok(27));
let result = <i32 as Num>::from_str_radix("foo", 10);
assert!(result.is_err());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-radices)Supported radices

The exact range of supported radices is at the discretion of each type implementation. For
primitive integers, this is implemented by the inherent `from_str_radix` methods in the
standard library, which **panic** if the radix is not in the range from 2 to 36. The
implementation in this crate for primitive floats is similar.

For third-party types, it is suggested that implementations should follow suit and at least
accept `2..=36` without panicking, but an `Err` may be returned for any unsupported radix.
It’s possible that a type might not even support the common radix 10, nor any, if string
parsing doesn’t make sense for that type.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

---

# NumAssign in num_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.19/trait.NumAssign.html

`pub trait NumAssign: `[Num](https://docs.rs/trait.Num.html) + [NumAssignOps](https://docs.rs/trait.NumAssignOps.html) { }## Expand description

The trait for `Num` types which also implement assignment operators.

This is automatically implemented for types which implement the operators.

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# RefNum in num_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.19/trait.RefNum.html

## Expand description

The trait for `Num` references which implement numeric operations, taking the
second operand either by value or by reference.

This is automatically implemented for all types which implement the operators. It covers
every type implementing the operations though, regardless of it being a reference or
related to `Num`.

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# clamp in num_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.19/fn.clamp.html

`pub fn clamp<T: `[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)>(input: T, min: T, max: T) -> T## Expand description

A value bounded by a minimum and a maximum

If input is less than min then this returns min. If input is greater than max then this returns max. Otherwise this returns input.

**Panics** in debug mode if `!(min <= max)`.

---

# clamp_max in num_traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/num-traits/^0.2.19/fn.clamp_max.html

`pub fn clamp_max<T: `[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)>(input: T, max: T) -> T## Expand description

A value bounded by a maximum value

If input is greater than max then this returns max.
Otherwise this returns input.
`clamp_max(std::f32::NAN, 1.0)` preserves `NAN` different from `f32::max(std::f32::NAN, 1.0)`.

**Panics** in debug mode if `!(max == max)`. (This occurs if `max` is `NAN`.)

---

# phf 0.13.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.13.1

# Rust-PHF

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.66.

## Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate.

To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
 = {  = "0.13.1",  = false }
```
### phf_macros

```
use phf_map;
static KEYWORDS: Map = phf_map! ;
// You can also use OR (`|`) patterns to map multiple keys to the same value:
static OPERATORS: Map = phf_map! ;
```
```
[]
 = {  = "0.13.1",  = ["macros"] }
```
#### Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

### phf_codegen

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[]
 = {  = "0.13.1",  = false }
 = "0.13.1"
```
Then put code on build.rs:

```
use env;
use File;
use ;
use Path;
```
and lib.rs:

```
include!;
```

---

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/latest/target-redirect/phf/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) by default and
also ships an experimental `ptrhash` feature for an alternative MPHF layout.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.85.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]
 phf = { version = "0.14.0", features = ["macros"] }
```
To try the experimental MPHF alternative instead of the default CHD layout,
enable the `ptrhash` feature on every `phf` crate involved in generation and
runtime lookup:

```
[dependencies]
phf = { version = "0.14.0", features = ["macros", "ptrhash"] }
```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.14.0", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_map/index.html)- map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_map](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_map.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Map`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_map.html)- ordered_ - map
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedMap`
- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_set.html)- ordered_ - set
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`OrderedSet`
- [phf_set](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_set.html)
- Macro to create a `static`(compile-time)`Set`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- An immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map
- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedSet.html)- Set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

# phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/phf/0.13.1/target-redirect/aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu/phf/

## Expand description

Rust-PHF is a library to generate efficient lookup tables at compile time using
[perfect hash functions](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perfect_hash_function).

It currently uses the
[CHD algorithm](http://cmph.sourceforge.net/papers/esa09.pdf) and can generate
a 100,000 entry map in roughly .4 seconds.

MSRV (minimum supported rust version) is Rust 1.66.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

PHF data structures can be constructed via either the procedural
macros in the `phf_macros` crate or code generation supported by the
`phf_codegen` crate. If you prefer macros, you can easily use them by
enabling the `macros` feature of the `phf` crate, like:

```
 [dependencies]
 phf = { version = "0.13.1", features = ["macros"] }
```
To compile the `phf` crate with a dependency on
libcore instead of libstd, enabling use in environments where libstd
will not work, set `default-features = false` for the dependency:

```
[dependencies]
# to use `phf` in `no_std` environments
phf = { version = "0.13.1", default-features = false }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-with-the-macros-feature-enabled)Example (with the `macros` feature enabled)

```
use phf::phf_map;
#[derive(Clone)]
pub enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = phf_map! {
    "loop" => Keyword::Loop,
    "continue" => Keyword::Continue,
    "break" => Keyword::Break,
    "fn" => Keyword::Fn,
    "extern" => Keyword::Extern,
};
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
Alternatively, you can use the [ phf_codegen](https://docs.rs/phf_codegen) crate to generate PHF datatypes
in a build script.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

Currently, the macro syntax has some limitations and may not
work as you want. See [#183](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/183) or [#196](https://github.com/rust-phf/rust-phf/issues/196) for example.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [map](https://docs.rs/map/index.html)

- An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.
- [ordered_](https://docs.rs/ordered_set/index.html)- set
- An order-preserving immutable set constructed at compile time.
- [set](https://docs.rs/set/index.html)
- An immutable set constructed at compile time.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [phf_](https://docs.rs/macro.phf_ordered_set.html)- ordered_ - set

# phf_codegen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf_codegen

## Expand description

A set of builders to generate Rust source for PHF data structures at compile time.

The provided builders are intended to be used in a Cargo build script to generate a Rust source file that will be included in a library at build time.

For more information about `rust-phf` crates, see [the  phf crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/phf).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

To use `phf_codegen` on build.rs, you have to add dependencies under `[build-dependencies]`:

```
[build-dependencies]
phf = { version = "0.14.0", default-features = false }
phf_codegen = "0.14.0"
```
When using the experimental `ptrhash` feature, enable it on both
`phf_codegen` and the runtime `phf` dependency so the generated constants
and runtime layout stay in sync.

Then put code on build.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
fn main() {
    let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
    let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
    write!(
        &mut file,
        "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static str, Keyword> = {}",
        phf_codegen::Map::new()
            .entry("loop", "Keyword::Loop")
            .entry("continue", "Keyword::Continue")
            .entry("break", "Keyword::Break")
            .entry("fn", "Keyword::Fn")
            .entry("extern", "Keyword::Extern")
            .build()
    )
    .unwrap();
    write!(&mut file, ";\n").unwrap();
}
```
and lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &str) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#byte-string-keys)Byte-String Keys

Byte strings by default produce references to fixed-size arrays; the compiler needs a hint to coerce them to slices:

build.rs:

```
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::{BufWriter, Write};
use std::path::Path;
let path = Path::new(&env::var("OUT_DIR").unwrap()).join("codegen.rs");
let mut file = BufWriter::new(File::create(&path).unwrap());
writeln!(
    &mut file,
     "static KEYWORDS: phf::Map<&'static [u8], Keyword> = \n{};\n",
     phf_codegen::Map::<&[u8]>::new()
         .entry(b"loop", "Keyword::Loop")
         .entry(b"continue", "Keyword::Continue")
         .entry(b"break", "Keyword::Break")
         .entry(b"fn", "Keyword::Fn")
         .entry(b"extern", "Keyword::Extern")
         .build()
).unwrap();
```
lib.rs:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#[derive(Clone)]
enum Keyword {
    Loop,
    Continue,
    Break,
    Fn,
    Extern,
}
include!(concat!(env!("OUT_DIR"), "/codegen.rs"));
pub fn parse_keyword(keyword: &[u8]) -> Option<Keyword> {
    KEYWORDS.get(keyword).cloned()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The compiler’s stack will overflow when processing extremely long method chains (500+ calls). When generating large PHF data structures, consider looping over the entries or making each call a separate statement:

```
let entries = [("hello", "1"), ("world", "2")];
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
for &(key, value) in &entries {
    builder.entry(key, value);
}
// ...
```
```
let mut builder = phf_codegen::Map::new();
builder.entry("hello", "1");
builder.entry("world", "2");
// ...
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayMap.html)- Map
- An adapter for printing a `Map`
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayOrderedMap.html)- Ordered - Map
- An adapter for printing a `OrderedMap`
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplayOrderedSet.html)- Ordered - Set
- An adapter for printing a `OrderedSet`
- [Display](https://docs.rs/struct.DisplaySet.html)- Set
- An adapter for printing a `Set`
- [Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html)
- A builder for the `phf::Map`type.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedMap.html)- Map
- A builder for the `phf::OrderedMap`type.
- [Ordered](https://docs.rs/struct.OrderedSet.html)- Set
- A builder for the `phf::OrderedSet`type.
- [Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html)
- A builder for the `phf::Set`type.

# phf_map in phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.13.1/macro.phf_map.html

`phf_map!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Macro to create a `static` (compile-time) [ Map](https://docs.rs/struct.Map.html).

Requires the `macros` feature.

Supported key expressions are:

- literals: bools, (byte) strings, bytes, chars, and integers (these must have a type suffix)
- arrays of `u8`integers
- tuples of any supported key expressions
- dereferenced byte string literals
- OR patterns using `|`to map multiple keys to the same value
- `UniCase::unicode(string)`,- `UniCase::ascii(string)`, or- `Ascii::new(string)`if the- `unicase`feature is enabled
- `UncasedStr::new(string)`if the- `uncased`feature is enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use phf::{phf_map, Map};
static MY_MAP: Map<&'static str, u32> = phf_map! {
    "hello" => 1,
    "world" => 2,
};
fn main () {
    assert_eq!(MY_MAP["hello"], 1);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#or-patterns)OR Patterns

You can use OR patterns to map multiple keys to the same value:

```
use phf::{phf_map, Map};
static OPERATORS: Map<&'static str, &'static str> = phf_map! {
    "+" | "add" | "plus" => "addition",
    "-" | "sub" | "minus" => "subtraction",
    "*" | "mul" | "times" => "multiplication",
};
fn main() {
    assert_eq!(OPERATORS["+"], "addition");
    assert_eq!(OPERATORS["add"], "addition");
    assert_eq!(OPERATORS["plus"], "addition");
}
```

---

# OrderedMap in phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.13.1/struct.OrderedMap.html

`pub struct OrderedMap<K: 'static, V: 'static> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An order-preserving immutable map constructed at compile time.

Unlike a `Map`, iteration order is guaranteed to match the definition
order.

[§](https://docs.rs#note)Note

The fields of this struct are public so that they may be initialized by the
`phf_ordered_map!` macro and code generation. They are subject to change at
any time and should never be accessed directly.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# phf_set in phf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/phf/^0.13.1/macro.phf_set.html

`phf_set!() { /* proc-macro */ }`## Expand description

Macro to create a `static` (compile-time) [ Set](https://docs.rs/struct.Set.html).

Requires the `macros` feature.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use phf::{phf_set, Set};
static MY_SET: Set<&'static str> = phf_set! {
    "hello world",
    "hola mundo",
};
fn main () {
    assert!(MY_SET.contains("hello world"));
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#or-patterns)OR Patterns

You can use OR patterns to include multiple keys in a single entry:

```
use phf::{phf_set, Set};
static KEYWORDS: Set<&'static str> = phf_set! {
    "if" | "elif" | "else",
    "for" | "while" | "loop",
    "fn" | "function" | "def",
};
fn main() {
    assert!(KEYWORDS.contains("if"));
    assert!(KEYWORDS.contains("elif"));
    assert!(KEYWORDS.contains("else"));
    assert!(KEYWORDS.contains("for"));
}
```

# rgb 0.8.53 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rgb/0.8.53

`struct RGB` for [Rust](https://www.rust-lang.org)

Operating on pixels as weakly-typed vectors of `u8` is error-prone and inconvenient. It's better to use vectors of pixel structs. However, Rust is so strongly typed that *your* RGB pixel struct is not compatible with *my* RGB pixel struct. So let's all use mine :P

## Installation

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8.51"
```
## Usage

`RGB` and `RGBA` structs

The structs implement common Rust traits and a few convenience functions, e.g. `map` that repeats an operation on every subpixel:

```
use *; // Laziest way to use traits which add extra methods to the structs
let px = RGB ;
let inverted = px.map;
println!; // Display: rgb(0,255,0)
assert_eq!;
```
### Byte slices to pixel slices

For interoperability with functions operating on generic arrays of bytes there are functions for safe casting to and from pixel slices.

```
let raw = vec!;
let pixels: & = raw.as_rgb; /// Safe casts without copying
let raw_again = pixels.as_bytes;
```
Note: if you get an error about "no method named `as_bytes` found", add `use rgb::ComponentBytes`. If you're using a custom component type (`RGB<CustomType>`), implement `rgb::Pod` (plain old data) and `rgb::Zeroable` trait for the component (these traits are from [ bytemuck](https://lib.rs/bytemuck) crate).

## About colorspaces

*Correct* color management is a complex problem, and this crate aims to be the lowest common denominator, so it's intentionally agnostic about it.

However, this library supports any subpixel type for `RGB<T>`, and `RGBA<RGBType, AlphaType>`, so you can use them with a newtype, e.g.:

```
;
type LinearRGB = ;
```
`BGRA`, `ARGB`, `Gray`, etc.

There are other color types in `rgb::alt::*`. There's also an optional `serde` feature that makes all types (de)serializable.

## Roadmap to 1.0

The plan is to provide easy migration to v1.0. There will be a transitional v0.9 version released that will be mostly backwards-compatible with 0.8, and forwards-compatible with 1.0.

Planned changes:

- Types will be renamed to follow Rust's naming convention: `RGBA`→`Rgba`. The old names will continue to work as hidden aliases.
- The `Gray`and`GrayAlpha`types will change from tuple structs with`.0`to structs with named fields`.v`(value) and`.a`(alpha). Through a`Deref`trick both field names will work, but`.0`is going to be deprecated.
- `bytemuck::Pod`(conversions from/to raw bytes) will require color and alpha components to be the same type (i.e. it will work with- `Rgba<u8>`, but not- `Rgba<Newtype, DifferentType>`). Currently it's unsound if the alpha has a different size than color components.
- Many inherent methods will be moved to a new `Pixel`trait.

## Migration from 0.8 to 0.9

-
Update to the latest version of 0.8, and fix all deprecation warnings. - rename `.alpha()`to`.with_alpha()`
- rename `.map_c()`to`.map_colors()`

- rename
-
Change field access on `GrayAlpha`from`.0`and`.1`to`.v`and`.a`where possible.
-
Use the `bytemuck`crate for conversions from/to bytes instead of`ComponentBytes`trait. Disable the`as-bytes`feature if possible.
-
Don't enable `gbr`and`argb`features. All pixel types are enabled by default.
-
In generic code operating on pixels, add `Copy + 'static`bounds to the pixel types and/or their components.
-
Test your code with `rgb = { version = "0.8.46", features = ["unstable-experimental"] }`, which enables some of the future breaking changes on the older version. This feature flag is only for testing, and will be changed/removed in the future.
-
Avoid wildcard imports from `rgb::alt::*`, and avoid using`GRAY8`-`GRAYA16`type aliases.

---

# rgb 0.8.53 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rgb/0.8.53/source/

#
                    rgb 0.8.53

                `struct RGB/RGBA/etc.` for sharing pixels between crates + convenience methods for color manipulation.
Allows no-copy high-level interoperability. Also adds common convenience methods and implements standard Rust traits to make `RGB`/`RGBA` pixels and slices first-class Rust objects.

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.16/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.

- [NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html)

# defmt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/defmt/^0.3.8/

## Expand description

A highly efficient logging framework that targets resource-constrained devices, like microcontrollers.

Check out the defmt book at [https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com](https://defmt.ferrous-systems.com) for more
information about how to use it.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

This is a defmt-0.3 compatbility crate. It depends upon `defmt-1.0` and
re-exports the items that were available in `defmt-0.3`. This allows you to
mix defmt-0.3 and defmt-1.0 within the same compilation.

The `defmt` wire format might change between minor versions. Attempting to
read a defmt stream with an incompatible version will result in an error,
and any tool used to process that stream should first check for a symbol
named like `_defmt_version_ = X`, where X indicates the wire format version
in use.

Updating your version of defmt might mean you also have to update your
version of `defmt-print` or `defmt-decoder`.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [assert](https://docs.rs/macro.assert.html)
- Just like the `core::assert!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_eq.html)- eq
- Just like the `core::assert_eq!``defmt`is used to log the panic message
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_ne.html)- ne
- Just like the `core::assert_ne!``defmt`is used to log the panic message

- Generates a bitflags structure that can be formatted with defmt.
- [dbg](https://docs.rs/macro.dbg.html)
- Just like the `std::dbg!``defmt`is used to log the message at`TRACE`level.

- Logs data at *debug*level.

- Logs data at *error*level.

- Logs data at *warn*level.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Debug2](https://docs.rs/struct.Debug2Format.html)- Format
- An “adapter” type to feed `Debug`values into defmt macros, which expect`defmt::Format`values.
- [Display2](https://docs.rs/struct.Display2Format.html)- Format
- An “adapter” type to feed `Display`values into defmt macros, which expect`defmt::Format`values.

- Encode raw defmt frames for sending over the wire.

- An interned string created via `intern!`

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.200/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
